The Swift fox (Vulpes velox) exhibits a suite of life-history traits characteristic of small canids inhabiting the shortgrass and mixed-grass prairies of North America. Among the most fundamental measures of reproductive timing is the gestation period, which in this species lasts approximately 55 days [tg = approximately 55 days] at a temperature of 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C]. This developmental interval occurs at the species' typical core body temperature of 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C], reflecting the thermal conditions under which the gestating embryo undergoes organogenesis and growth. Field observations indicate that females typically whelp a single annual litter [F_R_i = single annual litter], with parturition occurring in underground dens during the spring months. The neonatal offspring, born in a relatively altricial state, exhibit a wet weight at birth of approximately 39.65 grams [Wwb = approximately 39.65 grams], a modest mass that underscores the considerable maternal investment still required during the subsequent weeks of lactation and den attendance.

Following parturition, the altricial pups remain entirely dependent on maternal milk and the warmth of the natal den for a sustained period. The transition to nutritional independence through the cessation of lactation, or weaning, is documented to occur at 46 days after birth [tx = 46 days after birth], a metric recorded under the typical physiological temperature regime of 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C]. This weaning age marks the point at which the young kits begin to consume solid food items, such as small rodents and insects, brought to the den by both parents. The pre-weaning interval is a period of rapid mass gain and sensorimotor development; by the conclusion of this phase, the juvenile fox is beginning to explore the immediate vicinity of the burrow entrance. This developmental milestone is critical for survival, as it precedes the period of independent foraging and eventual dispersal from the natal territory.

As the juvenile Swift fox continues its growth trajectory beyond the weaning stage, the attainment of reproductive capacity marks a significant transition in its life cycle. Puberty, or the onset of sexual maturity, is reached at approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth], a duration measured in free-ranging populations at the species' typical core body temperature of 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C]. This age corresponds roughly to twelve months, aligning with the species' annual breeding phenology; individuals born in one spring are physiologically capable of breeding the following spring. This maturation schedule is typical of small canids, falling between the more rapid development seen in some smaller foxes and the extended juvenile periods of larger wolves. Reaching this milestone involves significant hormonal changes and the development of functional gonads, preparing the young fox for its first potential reproductive season.

The growth and development of the Swift fox culminates in an ultimate wet weight that characterizes the fully grown adult. Adults of this species attain a maximal body mass of 2400 grams [Wwi = 2400 grams], a size that places Vulpes velox among the smaller members of the genus. This adult mass is reached after the juvenile growth phase decelerates, and it represents the body size at which energetic demands for maintenance, locomotion, and reproduction are met. Regarding the species' annual reproductive output, breeding females produce approximately 4.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 4.5 pups per litter] in a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], a reproductive pattern typical for temperate-zone canids. Field data from the shortgrass prairie suggest that this single yearly litter is timed to coincide with peak prey availability in the spring.

A comprehensive view of the Swift fox's life-history strategy must also consider its overall lifespan, which dictates the number of potential reproductive cycles available to an individual. Maximum longevity in the wild, representing the complete duration from birth to natural mortality, has been recorded at approximately 15.9 years [am = approximately 15.9 years], a lifespan documented in populations inhabiting the species' thermal neutral zone at 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C]. This extended period of potential reproductive activity, when integrated with the annual single-litter frequency, yields a lifetime reproductive output that is substantial for a canid of this moderate body size. However, many individuals in wild populations succumb earlier due to predation, disease, or intraspecific competition before reaching this extreme age. The interplay between a relatively delayed puberty, a modest litter frequency, and a potentially long reproductive window defines a life-history strategy adapted to the variable and often harsh conditions of the North American prairie ecosystem, where the ability to survive multiple breeding seasons can offset the constraints of small litter size.
